input.question: Why a flight going East to West takes longer than exact same flight going West to East?
input.ground_truth: Because over a given part of the earth the wind moves predominantly in one direction . Hence one way the plane is flying into the wind and one it's flying with the wind. At the altitude of airliners the wind speeds constitute a noticeable fraction of the nominal speed of the aircraft - hence the difference. EDIT: I should have added that for this reason I wouldn't expect to see the affect you're describing on a generally north-south routing (eg london - cape town).

Okay! Imagine the Earth is like a big, round merry-go-round that’s spinning. When you want to fly from one side to another, the Earth is moving underneath you.

Let’s say you want to fly from New York (on the East coast of the USA) to Los Angeles (on the West coast).

If you fly **West to East** (with the spin), it’s like you’re walking the same way the merry-go-round is turning. The Earth helps you a little bit, so you get there a bit faster.

But if you fly **East to West** (against the spin), it’s like you’re walking backwards on the merry-go-round. The Earth is kind of pushing against you, so it takes a little longer to get there.

That’s why a flight going East to West usually takes a bit longer than the same flight going West to East! 🌍✈️
